knownFor: A teacher in the church at Rome in the early 200s who wrote in Greek. In his Refutation of All Heresies, a book against every teaching he held false, he attacked the bishop Callistus, and in 235 he was deported to Sardinia with Rome's bishop.
shortDescription: Hippolytus taught in the church at Rome in the early 200s and wrote in Greek. He held that the Son was another beside the Father, yet one God with him, would not give way to two bishops of Rome on this or on forgiveness, and in 235 was sent to Sardinia with Rome's bishop.
datesNote: No old source gives the year of his birth or of his death. He taught at Rome while Zephyrinus was bishop and after Callistus took his place. Rome's list of bishops, in the book of 354, dates his deportation to Sardinia by the consuls of the year, Severus and Quintianus, which is 235. Eusebius says his Easter table ran to the first year of the emperor Alexander.
placeNote: Rome, where he taught; Sardinia, to which he was deported with Rome's bishop; the Tiburtine Road, where Rome's calendar of martyrs places him.
role: Teacher and writer in the church at Rome. Rome's list of bishops calls him an elder; Eusebius says he led another church, and Jerome and Theodoret call him a bishop.

keyWorks.title: Refutation of All Heresies
keyWorks.about: a long book that traces every teaching he held false back to the Greek philosophers, the mystery cults and the astrologers. Its last part turns to the teachings of his own day at Rome, Callistus's among them, and it ends with his own account of the truth. It survives in one manuscript, found on Mount Athos in 1842 and printed in 1851 under the name of Origen; that it is his rests on its modern editors

keyWorks.title: Against Noetus
keyWorks.about: a work against Noetus of Smyrna, who taught that Christ was the Father himself, so that the Father was born, suffered and died. It answers that the Son is another beside the Father, yet one power with him: one God, in two persons, with the grace of the Holy Spirit as a third. Its manuscript calls it a homily of Hippolytus

keyWorks.title: On the Passover
keyWorks.about: a book named by Eusebius and Jerome, with a table of dates and a cycle of sixteen years for finding the day of Easter. Eusebius says the table ran to the first year of the emperor Alexander, and Jerome that it gave Eusebius the occasion for his own nineteen-year cycle

traces: Eusebius found his writings kept in the church library at Aelia, that is Jerusalem. He wrote that many other books of his were kept by many people.
Eusebius and Jerome each list his books. Jerome's list includes commentaries on books of Scripture, Against Marcion, On the Passover and Against All Heresies.
Jerome says his sixteen-year Easter cycle gave Eusebius the occasion for a nineteen-year cycle of his own.
Epiphanius names him with Clement and Irenaeus among those who refuted the followers of Valentinus.

Theodoret quotes him as a witness of the faith, as "the Holy Hippolytus, Bishop and Martyr". In a letter he ranks him with Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus and Justin, most of whom, he says, were both bishops and martyrs.

Writing to Damasus, bishop of Rome, Jerome gives the words of Hippolytus the martyr on Isaac's blessing. Elsewhere he calls him eloquent, and says that Ambrose's book on the six days of creation followed the views of Hippolytus and Basil.
remembered: Rome's calendar of martyrs, in the book of 354, keeps him on 13 August, on the Tiburtine Road, and Pontianus on the same day, in the cemetery of Callistus.

Damasus, bishop of Rome, set a verse on his tomb, telling what he had heard. It says that Hippolytus, an elder, had stayed in the split of Novatus, and that as he went to the kingdom of the faithful he told the people to follow the catholic faith, the faith of the whole church. So, the verse says, he earned his place as a martyr.

The poet Prudentius, in a hymn, tells of finding the tomb of Hippolytus, an elder who had once had a part in the split of Novatus. In the poem the judge has him torn apart by wild horses, the death of Hippolytus son of Theseus in the old Greek story.
The later Book of the Popes says that Pope Hadrian restored the cemetery of the blessed martyr Hippolytus, beside Saint Lawrence, which had decayed since early times.

uncertain: One witness. The quarrel with Zephyrinus and Callistus is known only from Hippolytus's own Refutation. It is an enemy's account, so what it says Callistus taught and ruled rests on him alone.

Callistus's side, as Hippolytus reports it. Callistus held that the Father and the Son are one Spirit, and that the Father suffered along with the Son. For his rule on sin he cited Paul's question about judging another man's servant, the parable of the wheat and the weeds, and Noah's ark, which held animals clean and unclean.

Who wrote the Refutation. Its one manuscript bore the name of Origen, and no old source names it among Hippolytus's books. Eusebius and Jerome name a book of his Against All Heresies. That the Refutation is his rests on its modern editors.

Elder or bishop. Rome's list of bishops calls him an elder, one of the priests who led the church with its bishop. Eusebius says he led another church, without saying which. Jerome calls him bishop of a church whose city he could not learn, and Theodoret calls him bishop and martyr.

His own claim. In the Refutation he counts himself and his side as the apostles' successors, sharing in their grace, their high priesthood and their teaching. The high priesthood was the church's chief priestly office. His English translator notes that the words may not mean a bishop's office only.

His side and Callistus's. Hippolytus says some whom his side had judged and put out of the church went over to Callistus. He calls Callistus's following a school, a teacher's following set up against the church, and its people Callistians. They, he says, "attempt to call themselves a Catholic Church", the church of the whole.

The split of Novatus. Damasus says he tells what he has heard. No old source we hold says whom he meant by Novatus. Rome's list of bishops names Novatus as the man who split Novatian off from the church at Rome, in the time of the bishop Cornelius. By the list's own dates that split came in 251, sixteen years after the exile.
His death. No old source tells how or where he died. Rome's calendar keeps him among its martyrs. The wild horses are Prudentius's legend.
Origen. Jerome says one of Hippolytus's sermons, On the praise of our Lord and Saviour, shows him speaking in church with Origen present. Jerome does not say when.

The third in God. In Against Noetus he speaks of one God, in two persons, with the grace of the Holy Spirit as a third. The Greek makes the Spirit's grace a third in God's ordering of things, which the English prints as economy.

The statue. A seated marble statue was found on the Tiburtine Road in 1551. Its chair carries tables for the day of Easter, in cycles of sixteen years, and a list of books. Its tie to Hippolytus is a modern identification.
Photius, writing centuries later, calls him a pupil of Irenaeus.

timeline.headline: Noetus of Smyrna before the elders

lines.text: Noetus, a man of Smyrna, teaches that Christ is the Father himself, so that the Father was born, suffered and died. Hippolytus says he lived not very long before.
lines.reference: Against Noetus 1, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 23116-23126 and 23141-23144; Greek, cic/texts/hippolytus_quae-feruntur-omnia-contra-noetum-grc_lagarde1858.txt lines 3181-3185

lines.text: The elders, the church's priests, call him before the church twice. The second time he asks what harm he is doing by glorifying Christ, and they put him out.

timeline.when: In the times of Victor and Zephyrinus, bishops of Rome
timeline.headline: The teaching reaches Rome, and he will not give way
timeline.witness: Hippolytus, in the Refutation, an enemy's account of Zephyrinus and Callistus

lines.text: Callistus, a servant of Carpophorus, loses money that widows and brethren had left at his bank and runs away. Later the city prefect sends him to a mine in Sardinia, and he is freed with other prisoners there through Marcia, who had asked the emperor Commodus for their release.
Zephyrinus makes Callistus his fellow worker in running the clergy and puts him in charge of the cemetery.
Epigonus, a pupil of Noetus, spreads Noetus's teaching at Rome, and Cleomenes, another disciple, strengthens it.
Zephyrinus lets the teaching spread for gain, Hippolytus says, and comes round to it himself, with Callistus as his adviser.
Hippolytus and his side refuse to go along with them and stand against them for the truth.
lines.reference: Refutation IX.6 and 7, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 13302-13304 and 13627-13633; Greek, cic/texts/hippolytus_refutatio-omnium-haeresium-grc_wendland-gcs26-1916.txt lines 18079-18081

lines.text: Callistus calls Hippolytus and his side worshippers of two gods, because they would not go along with him.

timeline.headline: His answer to Noetus: another beside the Father, yet one God

lines.text: He answers that Christ said he and the Father are one, and not that he is one with the Father as a single person: the words speak of two persons and one power.
As to power, he writes, God is one; as to God's ordering of things, there is a threefold showing.
He calls the Son another beside the Father, yet not a second God: as light from light, water from a spring, or a ray from the sun, one power from the whole.
He imagines someone asking whether he speaks of two Gods, and answers that he speaks of one God, in two persons, with the grace of the Holy Spirit as a third.
Jerome says one of his sermons shows him speaking in church with Origen present.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 61, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40701-40703; Latin, cic/texts/jerome_opera-pl23-part1-with-regula-pachomii-lat_migne1883.txt lines 56689-56692
lines.note: Jerome, writing long after, gives no date.

timeline.headline: Callistus bishop, and the quarrel over forgiveness
timeline.witness: Hippolytus, in the Refutation, an enemy's account of Callistus

lines.text: Callistus takes his place as bishop.
Callistus teaches that the Father and the Son are one Spirit, so that the Father suffered along with the Son.
Callistus forgives every sin of the body to anyone who comes over to him, and holds that a bishop should not be removed even for the gravest sin.
Some whom Hippolytus's side had judged and put out of the church go over to Callistus.
Hippolytus calls Callistus's following a school set up against the church, and its people Callistians; they call themselves a Catholic Church.

timeline.headline: His books: the Refutation, and a table for Easter

lines.text: In the Refutation he traces each teaching he held false back to the Greek philosophers, the mystery cults and the astrologers, and not to Scripture or to any saint's succession.
In its opening he counts himself and his side as the apostles' successors, sharing in their grace, their high priesthood and their teaching.
Its last part turns to the teachings of his own day, Callistus's among them.
The book ends with his account of the truth, and tells the reader that whoever obeys God will be like him, having been made divine.
He draws up a table, on a cycle of sixteen years, for finding the day of Easter; Eusebius says it ran to the first year of the emperor Alexander.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.22, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 35650-35651 and 35778-35780; Greek, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 4098-4102

lines.text: Christians then differed over the day: the churches of Asia kept the moon's fourteenth day, and Hippolytus counts those who kept the fourteenth day, whatever day of the week it fell, among the heretics.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V.23, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 31136-31140; Refutation VIII.11, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 13064-13075

timeline.when: 235, the year of the consuls Severus and Quintianus
timeline.headline: Deported to Sardinia with Rome's bishop
timeline.witness: Rome's list of bishops, in the book of 354

lines.text: Pontianus, the bishop, and Hippolytus, the elder, are deported as exiles to Sardinia, which the list calls an unhealthy island. It gives no reason.

lines.text: On the island Pontianus steps down, and Antheros is ordained in his place.
lines.reference: The list of the bishops of Rome, Pontianus, cic/texts/liber-pontificalis_texte-introduction-commentaire-t1-lat-fra_duchesne1886.txt lines 66808-66810

lines.text: Rome's calendar of martyrs keeps Hippolytus, on the Tiburtine Road, and Pontianus, in the cemetery of Callistus, on the same day.

The long-lost Refutation is found in a manuscript on Mount Athos.

briefReferences: Hippolytus, Against Noetus 1, tr. S. D. F. Salmond, with the Greek of Paul de Lagarde: Noetus of Smyrna, who said Christ was the Father himself, born, suffering and dying; called twice before the church by the elders and put out.

Against Noetus and the Refutation of All Heresies, both in Greek. Refutation IX.6 and 7, tr. J. H. MacMahon: Zephyrinus and Callistus on Noetus's teaching; his side would not give way. Against Noetus 11: the Son another beside the Father, yet one power. Rome's list of bishops in the book of 354: the deportation of 235 with Pontianus. The calendar of martyrs: 13 August.

Refutation IX.7: Epigonus and Cleomenes at Rome, Zephyrinus letting the teaching spread, Callistus his adviser; Hippolytus and his side withstanding them for the truth. The only account of the quarrel is his own.

Against Noetus 11, from Lagarde's Greek, confirmed by Salmond's English: light from light, water from a spring, a ray from the sun, one power, the Word. Against Noetus 14: one God, two persons, the grace of the Holy Spirit as a third. John 1:1 for the Word.
Refutation IX.6, Wendland's Greek and MacMahon's English: while Zephyrinus lived, Callistus called them worshippers of two gods, because they would not go along with him.

Refutation IX.7: after Zephyrinus's death, Callistus in his place; every sin forgiven to those who came over to him; a bishop not removed even for a sin unto death; some whom Hippolytus's side had put out went over to Callistus.

Refutation, preface, in Wendland's Greek and MacMahon's English: teachings traced to Greek philosophy, mysteries and astrologers; the apostles received the Holy Spirit and handed it on; their successors in grace, high priesthood and teaching. Refutation IX, opening: the teachings of his own day.

Eusebius, Church History VI.22: the work on the passover with its sixteen-year table. Eusebius, Church History V.23.1 and Refutation VIII.11: the fourteenth day. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 61: the cue to Eusebius's nineteen-year cycle.

Rome's list of bishops in the book of 354, under Pontianus, as printed by Duchesne: Pontianus the bishop and Hippolytus the elder deported to Sardinia in 235. The calendar of martyrs: both on 13 August. Eusebius, Church History VI.20: he led another church. Theodoret, Eranistes: holy bishop and martyr.

Damasus, verse on the tomb of Hippolytus, as printed by Duchesne in the Liber pontificalis: what Damasus had heard; the split of Novatus; the kingdom of the faithful; the catholic faith; his place as a martyr. Rome's list of bishops, under Fabian and Cornelius: the split of Novatian's party, in 251.

quotationOriginals.modern: When I say 'another,' I do not mean two Gods. I mean it as light from light, or water from a spring, or a ray from the sun. For there is one power, which comes from the whole. The whole is the Father, and from him comes the power, the Word.
quotationOriginals.printed: But when I say another, I do not mean that there are two Gods, but that it is only as light of light, or as water from a fountain, or as a ray from the sun. For there is but one power, which is from the All; and the Father is the All, from whom cometh this Power, the Word.
quotationOriginals.work: Hippolytus, Against Noetus 11, tr. S. D. F. Salmond; Greek ed. Paul de Lagarde
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The modern English is rendered from Lagarde's Greek, lines 3705 to 3708 of its file, which reads by hand ἕτερον δὲ λέγων οὐ δύο θεοὺς λέγω, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς ἢ ὡς ὕδωρ ἐκ πηγῆς ἢ ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἀπὸ ἡλίου. δύναμις γὰρ μία ἡ ἐκ τοῦ παντός, τὸ δὲ πᾶν πατήρ, ἐξ οὗ δύναμις λόγος. The scan is damaged there: it prints ix for ἐκ, Ἡ and ἡ for ἢ, and ἀκτῆα for ἀκτῖνα, with a line of stray marks inside the sentence, so the Greek is not printed here; Salmond's English confirms the reading. The words I mean it as supply the verb the Greek leaves understood in the second clause.

quotationOriginals.modern: We are their successors. We share in the same grace, in the high priesthood and in the teaching, and we are counted guardians of the church. We do not let our eyes droop, and we do not keep the right word silent.
quotationOriginals.printed: But we, as being their successors, and as participators in this grace, high-priesthood, and office of teaching, as well as being reputed guardians of the Church, must not be found deficient in vigilance, or disposed to suppress correct doctrine.
quotationOriginals.work: Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies, preface, tr. J. H. MacMahon; Greek ed. Paul Wendland
quotationOriginals.original: ὧν ἡμεῖς διάδοχοι τυγχάνοντες τῆς τε αὐτῆς χάριτος μετέχοντες ἀρχιερατείας τε χαὶ διδασκαλίας zal φρουροὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας λελογισμένοι οὐκ ὀφϑαλμῷ νυστάζομεν οὐδὲ λόγον ὀρϑὸν σιωπῶμεν
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is printed as the scan reads it; for χαὶ and zal it reads καὶ. The modern English follows Wendland's Greek, with the verbs in the present, we do not let our eyes droop and we do not keep silent, where MacMahon's English follows the future reading. Their means the apostles and those to whom they handed on the Holy Spirit, as the sentence before it says.
